questions.question: How do you properly close files in Go using defer?
questions.title: Defer Close Pattern
questions.direct_answer: defer f.Close() immediately after acquiring the file — it runs on every exit path (normal, early return, panic). The rule: acquisition and cleanup at the same scope, defer connecting them.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    O[os.Open] --> ERR{error?}
    ERR -->|yes| R[return — nothing acquired]
    ERR -->|no| D[defer f.Close]
    D --> WORK[work with f]
    WORK --> RET[any return]
    RET --> C[Close runs — always]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The Close's own failure mode: for a file being WRITTEN, Close flushes OS buffers — if the disk is full or permissions changed, Close fails and data is lost. The read-only case never fails meaningfully. The write case's contract: the data isn't durable until Close succeeds — that's why the write path's Close error is part of the operation's result, not cleanup noise.

The scope-coupling design: Go's defer binds cleanup to the scope of acquisition — as long as Open and Close are in the same function, the defer guarantees pairing. The pattern breaks when Open escapes the scope (returning an open file — now the CALLER owns the close). The explicit-ownership pattern for that: document it (io.Closer interfaces, 'the caller must Close').

The resource-leak math that motivates the discipline: Go's GC eventually finalizes files, but not before running out of file descriptors. The default ulimit (often 1024) means ~1024 concurrent unclosed files hang the process. In a long-running server, one unclosed file per request = a few hours to a crash.
